item.title: Human and chimpanzee leaders share a taste for risk
item.description: People in leadership positions tend to rate themselves as more risk-loving than those without leadership responsibilities—and a similar pattern emerges among chimpanzees: High-ranking individuals are perceived as more risk-taking than their lower-ranking peers. This is the conclusion of a new study by researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, Dresden University of Technology, and the University of Portsmouth, published in The Leadership Quarterly. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: GenAI and travel planning: Should AI agents build our itineraries?
item.description: Whether you're a seasoned tourist or an emerging explorer, delegating travel planning to artificial intelligence (AI) agents is becoming the norm for many travelers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Perseverance offers clues to protect crews from ultrafine Mars dust
item.description: Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA's Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are carried aboard the rover, including particles small enough to penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and could inform spacesuit and habitat design, dust-removal procedures and crew health standards for future NASA missions to Mars. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Election forecasters lack historical data on how national mood drives each senate race, study shows
item.description: U.S. Senate races are increasingly decided by national forces rather than state-level politics or incumbency advantage. That makes election forecasts less certain than they appear, according to a new study in PS: Political Science & Politics by researchers at the University of California, Davis, and George Mason University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How AI planning could create financial market fragility
item.description: Wharton experts are raising concerns about AI-driven financial market manipulation and runaway technology in a new paper titled "Financial Market Fragility in the Era of AI Planning." Finance professor Winston (Wei) Dou, finance and economics professor Itay Goldstein and Hong Kong University finance professor Yan Ji demonstrate how AI planning technologies could pave the way for collusive trading and increase financial market fragility. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth may have formed much of its water as the planet grew
item.description: Earth may have produced much of its water during the planet's formation, as rocky pebbles reacted with the hydrogen-rich atmosphere surrounding the young planet, according to new research published in Nature Geoscience. The findings offer a potential explanation for how Earth acquired one of the essential ingredients for life and suggest that similar water-producing processes could be common on rocky planets beyond our solar system. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reveal the staggering number of bat deaths at wind turbines
item.description: Bat populations across the United States face numerous threats, and one of the biggest may be the number of collisions with wind turbines. According to the most comprehensive study of the problem to date, published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, more than 18 million bats may have died at wind energy facilities between 1981 and 2024. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 121-million-year-old fossils suggest Longipteryx had no tail feathers
item.description: Around 121 million years ago, somewhere in modern northeastern China, an early bird took to the skies. If you drew its silhouette, you'd notice something was missing. Unlike any bird alive today, it had no tail feathers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The upside of untidiness: Why a little mess can be good for your home
item.description: If we're to follow the philosophy of organizer extraordinaire Marie Kondo, a tidy home is a better home. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Radio images reveal disturbances from Betelgeuse's mysterious companion that lurks within its shadows
item.description: The well-known star Betelgeuse has a mysterious houseguest—and it's shaking the rafters, rattling the pipes and slamming the cupboards (metaphorically speaking). It's causing enough subtle atmospheric disturbance that it might as well be making ghost noises. Who's to blame? New data suggest that its recently discovered companion star, Siwarha, is the one doing the haunting. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Technician cracks 1,600-year-old mystery to replicate color-changing effect of Roman glass masterpiece
item.description: The Lycurgus Cup, a world-renowned 4th-century A.D. artifact housed in the British Museum, is constructed of "dichroic" glass that shifts from jade green in reflected light to ruby red in transmitted light. This means that depending on where the light source is positioned, observers can see the cup displayed in two distinctive, contrasting colors. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Marine molecule may help combat 'brain-eating' amoeba
item.description: Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), a parasitic disease that causes the rapid deterioration of brain tissue, is one of the most lethal infections known, with a fatality rate exceeding 97%. Caused by the free-living amoeba Naegleria fowleri (N. fowleri), the disease progresses with devastating speed, often leaving patients with only a few days to respond to treatment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The mathematics of growing a shell—recreating diverse mollusk shells with just three inputs
item.description: Kaushik Bhattacharya is an engineer and materials scientist, but he has always been fascinated by seashells. Part of the draw is the "beautiful" idea that even simple organisms like mollusks can construct wonderfully complex structures over and over again, even in differing environments. He marvels at nature's engineering capabilities. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: MIT students tackle lunar waste with recycling system
item.description: MIT students have pioneered a revolutionary recycling solution aimed at mitigating waste buildup on the Moon. As new supplies begin to arrive, it is vital to have efficient methods for dealing with packaging waste. This ambitious project, which has garnered accolades from NASA, seeks to transform waste into useful materials for lunar bases, setting a precedent for potential sustainability improvements both on the Moon and Earth. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: See no evil: How willful ignorance supports the illegal tobacco trade
item.description: Adopting a "don't ask, don't tell" approach to illicit tobacco enables people to avoid thinking about where cheap smokes come from, researchers at the University of Otago, Wellington, have found. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anyone Can Dock: Molecular docking platform brings protein-binding predictions to smartphones, tablets and computers
item.description: A new platform, developed by researchers at the Center for Computational Sciences, University of Tsukuba, in collaboration with Mahidol University, makes molecular docking easier to access, understand, and integrate into experimental research. The work is published in the Journal of Cheminformatics. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Italian archaeologists discover links to tomb of Jesus underneath Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre
item.description: Italian researchers have found a burial ground beneath Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre, matching biblical accounts of the location of Jesus' burial. Fuente: Euronews.

item.title: Greenhouse gas levels hit new record highs in 2025: UN
item.description: Greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere rose to new record highs in 2025, locking in climate impacts that will persist for centuries to come, the United Nations said Tuesday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Colorado's glaciers thinned dramatically due to record-low snow and heat in 2026
item.description: The most prominent glaciers in Colorado thinned dramatically over the past year due to record-low mountain snow and record-warm temperatures, according to new research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Webb links interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS to worlds beyond Neptune through similar ice signatures
item.description: A Southwest Research Institute–led study used NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to examine ice grains streaming from interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS, just the third object from beyond our solar system ever identified. The observations point to tiny aggregates of water ice and dust, about a micron or smaller. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Crowdsourced collaborations: Using AI, social media to find potential brand partners
item.description: Brand collaborations have been growing in popularity as a powerful marketing tool for businesses looking to generate hype and expand their customer base, but brand managers often rely on costly and time-consuming surveys and screenings to identify potential matchups. A recent study by a Penn State researcher and collaborators proposes a new method: an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered framework that can uncover promising brand collaborations by leveraging the social media chatter of consumers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: First light: Hera resolves two asteroids instead of one
item.description: The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft for planetary defence has resolved its two target asteroids separately for the very first time, revealing the binary nature of the Didymos system, currently some 197 million km away from Earth. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: NASA astronaut Christina Koch on life in space, humanity and her African connection
item.description: In an exclusive interview with Africanews on the sidelines of the ceremony, Koch reflected on how seeing Earth from space changed her perspective on humanity, global cooperation and the importance of diversity in exploration. Fuente: Africanews.
item.dc:creator: editorial@africanews.com (michael oduor)

item.title: Lean Six Sigma framework for developing doctoral research problem statements outlined in white paper
item.description: University of Phoenix College of Doctoral Studies has published a new white paper, "Building a Lean Six Sigma–Based Background of the Problem and Problem Statement," by James C. Rice, DM/IST, MBA, and Scott A. McCalla, DM, MA. The paper presents an author-developed framework that adapts the Define and Measure logic of Lean Six Sigma to help doctoral practitioner researchers develop a defensible background of the problem and problem statement grounded in authoritative evidence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sculpture recreates odd optical effects of famed Lycurgus Cup
item.description: University of Sheffield researchers figured out how to recreate the 1600-year-old glass recipe. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Ouellette

item.title: Mathematical puzzle from 1904 takes physical form in gold-studded helium droplets
item.description: When identical charges repel each other but are confined to the surface of a sphere, they seek the arrangement with the lowest possible energy. The idea is simple, but the problem gets harder to solve with every charge added. The so-called Thomson problem dates back to the "plum-pudding" model of the atom, which Nobel laureate Joseph J. Thomson proposed in 1904. The atomic model has long been superseded, but the mathematical problem has endured. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Millipede from South Australia rediscovered and described 90 years after it was first collected
item.description: The new species Colobothrix deckeri is in the millipede family Dalodesmidae. It is remarkable because it is the first in its moisture-loving family to be found in a part of Australia with a low annual rainfall, between 400 and 500 mm (16 and 20 inches). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nano-wrinkles and actuation break up infectious biofilms on implants
item.description: A nano-wrinkled surface combined with a tiny soft actuator can break up infection-causing bacterial sheets, called biofilms, that form on medical implants, according to a University of Michigan Engineering study published in Advanced Functional Materials. When implanted in mice, the platform—called DARTS (dynamically actuated reconfigurable topographical surface)—reduced bacterial burden and improved the surrounding tissue response. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reveal hidden world of living cells in human milk
item.description: Advanced nanoscale imaging technology has revealed the diversity of living cells in human milk and uncovered new insights into how these cells are structured, what they contain and how they use nutrients. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'Porous anchor' that strongly bonds dissimilar materials formed simply by coating and drying
item.description: The National Institute for Materials Science has developed a technology to strongly bond dissimilar materials by using a porous layer, formed by a solution-coating and drying process, as an anchor. The research team confirm that even materials that are normally difficult to bond together can be bonded with a strength exceeding 7 MPa by adopting a hybrid approach: adhering to one material through chemical affinity and bonding to another via physical interlocking using tiny pores. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New converter could bridge light wavelength gap in quantum communications
item.description: Quantum networks, systems that connect devices using quantum mechanical effects, could potentially allow users to share information more securely and efficiently. Building these networks typically entails linking stationary qubits, units of quantum information encoded in trapped ions or other physical systems, using photons (particles of light) transmitted through optical fibers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Los gases de efecto invernadero alcanzaron un nuevo récord y advierten por el impacto que tendrá El Niño
item.description: Desde la ONU advirtieron que estos gases retienen calor en la atmósfera y eso aumentará las temperaturas a largo plazo. Habrá un nuevo aumento de las concentraciones de gases en 2026 por la quema de combustibles fósiles y el Super Niño. Fuente: Clarín - Mundo.
item.dc:creator: Clarin.com - Home

item.title: Record carbon dioxide levels will impact us for centuries, says UN weather agency
item.description: Levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases in the atmosphere caused by burning fossil fuels reached record highs in 2025, locking in more long-term global warming, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said on Tuesday. Fuente: UN News.

item.title: The secret to slower aging may be hiding in your gut
item.description: The secret to aging more slowly may be hiding in your gut. Scientists discovered that certain gut bacteria are strongly linked to how quickly the body ages, with microbial differences accounting for about 15% of the variation in biological aging rates. Some bacterial species were associated with slower aging, while others were linked to accelerated aging. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver
item.description: Scientists have discovered that low testosterone and a high-fructose diet can work together to worsen fatty liver disease in mice. Unexpectedly, changes in gut bacteria appear to drive this harmful interaction, revealing a potential new target for preventing liver damage. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body
item.description: A surprising discovery reveals that widely used anti-inflammatory drugs may unintentionally help dangerous viruses spread through the body. Scientists found that JAK inhibitors, prescribed for rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory diseases, can weaken a crucial immune defense against influenza, COVID-19, and other infections. By suppressing genes that normally fight viruses, these medications may leave patients more vulnerable to infection. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: La NASA revela los detalles de Artemis III, la misión que servirá de ensayo inmediatamente anterior para volver a la Luna
item.description: Los planes de la NASA para Artemis III han cambiado bastante desde que se concibió en un primer momento. Puesto que Artemis II ya sobrevoló la Luna , la lógica inicial era seguir en esa misma línea. Sin embargo, por la seguridad de los astronautas y para abaratar los costes, se optó por realizar todas las pruebas de la misión directamente en la órbita terrestre. Más allá de eso, hasta ahora no teníamos demasiada información sobre esta tercera fase del programa lunar. Sin embargo, el pasado 23 de octubre la NASA hizo un comunicado en el que describió paso a paso cuál será el plan y, por… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
item.description: A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen. The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: China eatery creates egg tarts topped with ‘giant cockroaches’, drawing widespread curiosity
item.description: A restaurant in Shunde, Guangdong, is turning heads online with a bizarre new dessert: egg tarts topped with crispy water beetles that look exactly like gigantic cockroaches. Shunde is a city known for its Cantonese cuisine and recognised as a Unesco Creative City of Gastronomy. In early October, it introduced a new “water roach egg tart”, priced at 28 yuan (US$4) for three. Images of the dessert, with a large insect perched on each tart, quickly made it a social media sensation. However,... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Fran Lu

item.title: ESA procures four new Galileo Second Generation satellites
item.description: The European Space Agency (ESA) has extended ongoing contracts to build four additional Galileo Second Generation (G2) satellites, ensuring the long-term continuity of the constellation and supporting the rollout of new services. With this procurement, the Galileo Second Generation fleet grows to 16 satellites. Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Smithsonian scientists just recreated the first 2 billion years of the Universe
item.description: Scientists have created one of the largest and most detailed simulations of the early universe ever made, offering an extraordinary new glimpse into the cosmos shortly after the Big Bang. Called Lumina, the groundbreaking simulation recreates the universe’s first 2 billion years, showing how dark matter, gas, and radiation interacted to give rise to the earliest stars, galaxies, and black holes. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: 13,800-year-old Alaska campsite reveals tools, a hearth and clues to early life near Beringia
item.description: Archaeological research at Shég’ Xdaltth’í’ in Alaska revealed a rich site dating back 13,800 years. The site included stone tools, animal remains, and evidence of a possible shelter. Researchers identified activities such as food processing, toolmaking, and clothing production among early inhabitants. Comparisons with similar tools in Siberia suggest cultural connections across the Bering Land Bridge. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: A tiny laser beam could make computer memory 1,000 times faster
item.description: Scientists at UC San Diego have developed a surprising new way to store digital information using light instead of magnets, potentially paving the way for smaller, faster, and more energy-efficient memory devices. By precisely shaping and shrinking an ultrafast laser beam, researchers demonstrated that they could switch magnetic states in a material, the basic process used to write digital data. The technique could potentially operate more than 1,000 times faster than conventional magnetic switching methods. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: India orders evacuations as Cyclone Arnab looms
item.description: Indian authorities ordered nearly 100,000 people to evacuate homes in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha ahead of a severe cyclone the national weather office expects to make landfall by Wednesday. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Anangu traditional owners and scientists join forces to understand mass plant dieback at Uluru
item.description: A new collaborative research project between Anangu, the traditional owners of Uluru, and plant scientists has uncovered the physiological traits that helped some species of desert plants survive a mass dieback event in Australia. These results reveal the key strategies for desert plant survival in the face of increasing extreme weather events, with consequences for the conservation of ecologically and culturally important keystone species. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How a Johnson Mentor Shapes the Next Generation of NASA Talent
item.description: When Rice University student Malvika Bhardwaj asked her mentor Daniel Cohen, a Guidance, Navigation & Control (GN&C) engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, whether he had time to keep teaching interns with his busy workload, he answered, “You decide what’s important.” In honor of National Mentoring Day on Oct. 27, Bhardwaj reflects on how Cohen’s […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Sumer Loggins

item.title: The price of romance: young Malaysian men borrow to fund dates, study finds
item.description: More than one in 10 Malaysian men have borrowed money to pay for dates, while nearly six in 10 usually pick up the entire bill, a survey has found. The findings come as rising living costs place a financial strain on romance in Malaysia, where money worries are increasingly complicating plans for marriage and starting a family. According to the Dating Expenditure Survey in Malaysia, released on Tuesday by independent policy research firm LEGASI Research, 13.2 per cent of male respondents... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Iman Muttaqin Yusof

item.title: China trial shows gum tissue stem cells help 55% of lifetime diabetes patients
item.description: A randomised phase one clinical trial conducted by scientists and doctors from Shanghai and Guangzhou has achieved encouraging results in the treatment of Type 1 diabetes using stem cells extracted from the mouth’s gum tissue. More than half of those who received the treatment showed varying degrees of improvement, while one subject was able to discontinue exogenous insulin therapy completely, the researchers said. Results of the study, which tested a therapy based on gingival mesenchymal stem... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Shi Huang

item.title: Q&A: Why does the right side of the brain control the left side of the body?
item.description: Dr. Martin Wessendorf is a neuroscientist and an associate professor emeritus at the University of Minnesota. His work focuses on how the brainstem controls the function of neurons in the spinal cord. Daniel Wang also researches the brain, focusing on cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative diseases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Do spiders dream? Scientists just found a surprising clue
item.description: Scientists have discovered that spiders may sleep in ways surprisingly similar to humans, complete with distinct sleep stages and a dream-like REM state. Researchers at the University of Bonn studied the Australian jumping spider Portia fimbriata, a remarkably clever hunter known for its sophisticated strategies. By recording the spiders over several days and nights, they found clear evidence of regulated sleep, including a REM-like stage marked by eye movements and muscle twitches. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: APOD: 2026 October 27 – Noctilucent Clouds over Sweden
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 October 27 –… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. Noctilucent Clouds over […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists discover a surprising clue to why some brains resist Alzheimer’s
item.description: Why do some people stay mentally sharp even when their brains show signs of Alzheimer’s disease? Scientists in the Netherlands may have uncovered an important clue hidden in a rare group of immature brain cells. Researchers discovered that these cells remain present even in people over 80, but their behavior differs dramatically between those who develop dementia and those who remain cognitively healthy. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Chinese scientists create powerful catalyst to turn air on Mars into rocket fuel
item.description: Chinese space scientists are working out how future astronauts on Mars could make their own fuel out of thin air, a sign that Beijing is serious about one day sending people to the red planet. A team at the state-funded Deep Space Exploration Laboratory in Hefei has developed a catalyst that turns carbon dioxide – which makes up more than 95 per cent of the Martian atmosphere – into a liquid fuel called methanol. “Methanol can serve as fuel to generate electricity, provide heating and power Mars... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: A-81 Reaches South Georgia
item.description: The Antarctic iceberg made a relatively quick exit from the Weddell Sea, only to slow at the edge of a remote island’s underwater shelf. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Social media analysis reveals how international solidarity shifts during prolonged conflict
item.description: Some of the best research questions begin in the classroom. A new publication by political scientist A. Burcu Bayram and psychologist Vivian P. Ta-Johnson (UT San Antonio) in the journal Political Psychology is an example of how class discussions with engaged and insightful students can inspire innovative research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Skip-level meetings may win bypassed managers' support, but how they are done matters
item.description: Skip-level meetings (SLMs) seem common in some work environments but unheard of and norm-breaking in others. They entail both benefits and risks for employees, bypassed and skip-level managers, and organizations. Their effects also depend on context, as my qualitative exploratory study, published in IEEE Engineering Management Review, suggested. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging
item.description: Mayo Clinic scientists have uncovered surprising new insights into “zombie cells,” aging cells that linger in the body and contribute to inflammation and disease. Seven studies reveal why these cells are harmful and identify new strategies for targeting them, including a natural compound found in tomatoes. In aging mice, experimental treatments reduced inflammation and improved physical and brain health. The findings could open the door to therapies that combat some of the biological processes behind aging. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Stanford prison experiment: Why do controversial psychology studies still have such a hold on us?
item.description: Two of the most famous experiments in psychology, the Stanford prison experiment and Stanley Milgram's obedience studies, have been called a sham, a lie and a fraud. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Social media on travel platforms can boost Gen Z well-being when it encourages positive emotional engagement
item.description: Social media communication on online travel platforms may contribute to customer well-being when it encourages participation and positive emotional experiences, according to a study of 210 Generation Z users reported in the International Journal of Electronic Marketing and Retailing. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Long-term analysis questions whether Japan's depopulation policy can stabilize shrinking communities
item.description: Small and medium-sized cities (SMCs) are essential for balanced national development, yet many are now facing prolonged population loss, aging and weakened labor markets. Japan has addressed this challenge for more than half a century through the Depopulated-Area-Designation (DAD) policy, a national framework that identifies municipalities facing population loss and supports them through infrastructure, fiscal, industrial and social measures. However, it has not been determined whether such a designation can stabilize shrinking communities over time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 1.9-million-year-old discovery rewrites the story of human evolution
item.description: New evidence suggests that early humans reached the Jordan Valley at least 1.9 million years ago, hundreds of thousands of years earlier than scientists previously thought. Advanced dating methods revealed that the ‘Ubeidiya site is roughly as old as the famous Dmanisi site in Georgia, placing both among the earliest known human settlements outside Africa. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Global happiness researchers reveal keys to a good life
item.description: Many of the world's leading happiness researchers say they consciously spend more time with loved ones after seeing the evidence, according to a new paper. "Happiness emerges from a symphony of factors, but if I had to pinpoint one secret to happiness, relationships with other people might be it," says Lara Aknin, a professor of social psychology at Simon Fraser University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Cohere says Alibaba’s Qwen model tried to send a file to Beijing
item.description: An AI model said it wouldn’t use any tools, then tried to send something to a server in Beijing anyway, and while researchers say it’s probably a training quirk and not espionage, the whole thing has people asking how much to trust free Chinese AI. Fuente: TechCrunch.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Mehta

item.title: False lingzhi unmasked: Scientists crack the 245-year mystery behind a medicinal mushroom mix-up
item.description: In a new study published today in Plants, People, Planet, scientists from the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, and their international collaborators clarify the distinction between Ganoderma lucidum, a European bracket fungus described in 1781, and Ganoderma lingzhi, the East Asian species widely associated with medicinal lingzhi or reishi. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Taiwan looks to autonomous swarms to counter Beijing’s grey-zone pressure
item.description: Taiwan is developing an AI-powered system to coordinate drone fleets for maritime surveillance and countering “grey-zone” activities, with researchers completing a simulation involving 20 aircraft, according to the island’s Ocean Affairs Council. The system, which is funded by the council, would allow different types of drones to autonomously divide tasks, plan routes and coordinate their movements while providing wide-area, persistent surveillance for coastguard operations. The council said on... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Lawrence Chung

item.title: The surprisingly simple exercise that could lower your blood pressure
item.description: A surprisingly simple exercise routine could help lower blood pressure without requiring daily workouts or expensive equipment. In a study of 100 adults, researchers found that wall squats performed just once or twice a week helped maintain significant reductions in systolic blood pressure over the short term. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Zoologist's study of wild Panamanian bats highlights use of metrics to inform bat conservation
item.description: Bats are not only a marvel of myth and imagination but also of energy use, working at the height of their energetic ceiling to fly the night skies the world over. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New online tool to help turn food waste into opportunity
item.description: Western Australian businesses can now make better-informed decisions about reducing food waste and turning discarded materials into valuable products, thanks to a new online toolkit. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fossils from brickworks reveal new dinosaur species that roamed England's wetlands 125 million years ago
item.description: More than 25 years after it was first discovered, a new species and genus of dinosaur have been named from the fossil collections cared for by the Natural History Museum. Paludohadros proudlovii was discovered at wienerberger's Ewhurst brick and roof tile works (Ewhurst Works) in Surrey in 2001 and subsequently donated to the Natural History Museum. It was a member of the iguanodontians—a group of dinosaurs known for their charismatic thumb spikes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 27 exoplanet targets for the world's first private space telescope
item.description: The Lazuli Space Telescope will be the first private space telescope. It's the brainchild of Eric Schmidt, Google's former CEO. It will have a 3-meter mirror (9.8 feet), larger than Hubble's 2.4-meter mirror (7.9 feet), and will be launched by 2029. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New binary gene expression system enables independent control of multiple cell types
item.description: Our bodies are composed of many different types of cells that work together to build and maintain normal physiological functions. In the central nervous system, for example, neurons transmit information, while glial cells such as astrocytes regulate the environment surrounding neurons and support their function. Understanding how these cell types influence one another is essential for uncovering how our bodies develop and function. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists solve a 30-year mystery behind inflammatory bowel disease
item.description: Scientists have identified a hidden cause of inflammatory bowel disease: antibodies that disable the immune system’s natural ability to control inflammation, potentially explaining severe illness in thousands of patients. The breakthrough also solves a 30-year genetic mystery and could pave the way for more precise diagnoses and targeted treatments. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: South Africa's lion-petting industry: We spent three years investigating and here's what we found
item.description: An estimated 8,000 lions are held in captivity in South Africa in about 350 places, ranging from zoos to tourism venues where people can interact up close with the big cats. Lions are also bred for live trade, trade in body parts and captive hunts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Inside the narcissistic brain: fMRI research sheds light on the narcissist's struggle with empathy
item.description: Many people have narcissistic traits to some degree, for example, confidence in one's own superiority, a sense of entitlement and a desire to be the center of attention. However, some people have notably higher levels of narcissistic traits than others, and the neural basis of so-called "grandiose narcissism" has rarely been studied in socially complex situations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Water into fuel: The new nanomaterial that could upgrade green hydrogen
item.description: Generating hydrogen without releasing carbon dioxide sounds simple: pass electricity through water, split water molecules and generate green hydrogen. The hard part is the electrocatalyst. The best ones rely on platinum, ruthenium and iridium, which are scarce and expensive. We wanted to know whether a small amount of iron and nickel oxides, anchored on carbon nanofibers grown by chemical vapor deposition the right way on the right scaffold, could do the job instead. Our results are published in ACS Applied Nano Materials. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Glowing ghoul or chemical tool? The toxic chemistry behind Victorian séances
item.description: In November 1857, during a séance in Jersey City, the medium Leah Brown claimed her body produced luminous particles. So intense was the luminosity emanating from her, she recalled in her memoir, that it almost burned her hands. She rinsed her hands under a tap and then pushed them into the damp earth outside. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance Views Dust at Neretva Vallis
item.description: Description This 360-degree look at Neretva Vallis within Mars’ Jezero Crater was stitched together using 217 images acquired by the rover’s Mastcam-Z on May 20, 2024, the 1,155th Martian day, or sol, of the mission. While it is a wind-swept dusty vista today, billions of years ago it was home to a river channel that fed fresh water into […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Spending in‑person time with friends is the biggest predictor of whether college students flourish
item.description: Exercise, avoiding alcohol or even getting enough sleep aren't the factors most connected to college students' well-being. Spending face-to-face time with friends and other people is the strongest predictor of their mental health, according to a 2026 study of nearly 80,000 students that I conducted with the help of my students. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could ecological roles offer clues to how life began?
item.description: Producers, consumers, and decomposers play different roles in today's ecosystems. Thinking about these familiar roles led me to a question: Could their differences partly reflect the different physical and chemical environments in which early life developed? I wondered whether the organization of ecosystems might offer a useful starting point for thinking about life's beginnings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Expanding hemp could boost Kentucky water quality and ecological diversity
item.description: Hemp has long been pitched to Kentucky farmers as a way to diversify their income. Research now suggests it could diversify the landscape itself, with measurable benefits for the state's water and wildlife. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Metalens microscope switches focus with voltage, not moving optics
item.description: Just as it is difficult for a camera to keep both a nearby flower and a distant mountain sharply focused at the same time, conventional optical microscopes face a similar challenge when imaging structures located at different depths inside the body. Tighter focusing of light improves spatial resolution, but at the same time reduces the depth range over which the image remains sharply focused. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Beyond trial and error: Integrating computation, processing, and AI to design high-entropy alloys
item.description: Designing structural high-entropy alloys (SHEAs) means solving a problem with an enormous number of moving parts: which combinations of composition and processing conditions will yield the phases, microstructures, and mechanical properties a given application demands? Because these alloys mix multiple principal elements in comparable proportions, that question spans length and time scales that no single experiment or model can cover on its own. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust
item.description: Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are carried aboard the rover, including some that are small enough to penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The findings will be published Tuesday, Oct. 27, in the Proceedings of […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Barnett

item.title: Silent bacterial genes yield potential leads for future cancer drugs
item.description: Natural products produced by microorganisms are a promising source of new drugs. Researchers at the Helmholtz Center for Infection Research (HZI) and its Saarbrücken-based site, the Helmholtz Institute for Pharmaceutical Research Saarland (HIPS), have now discovered a new family of such compounds, elucidated their unusual biosynthesis and developed a way to produce them synthetically. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Light-based monitoring could improve quality checks for lab-grown replacement cartilage
item.description: A new doctoral dissertation by Omar Anwar Elkadi in the field of Applied Physics on near-infrared spectroscopy for the continuous monitoring of tissue-engineered cartilage will be defended at the Faculty of Science, Forestry and Technology, Kuopio campus, of the University of Eastern Finland on Oct. 30. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NEO Surveyor’s Sunshade Gets Inspected
item.description: Description The large sunshade of NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor is mounted on an assembly ring during inspections in a clean room at BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Boulder, Colorado, in July 2026. The sunshade structure stands 20 feet (6 meters) tall and measures 8 feet (2.4 meters) wide at its base. Its two flat […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Solar Cells Inspected on NASA’s NEO Surveyor
item.description: Description The large sunshade of NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor mission is inspected by a technician at BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Boulder, Colorado, in late July. Built by Applied Aerospace in Stockton, California, the sunshade structure was outfitted with its solar cells by SolAero Technologies in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in January. Environmental […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Can cats really thrive on vegan diets? Professor Andrew Knight responds to critics
item.description: In response to a recent article on vegan diets for cats, Phys.org received numerous messages from concerned readers. People raised a lot of concerns, mainly arguing that cats are obligate carnivores and that vegan diets could be very harmful to their health. Now, we have collected all these comments, questions and concerns and asked the researcher behind the original paper to address them. Andrew Knight, Veterinary Professor of Animal Welfare and Associate Professor at Murdoch University School of Veterinary Medicine, offers his response below. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Is masculinity a barrier to green jobs? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Las muestras que OSIRIS-REx trajo del asteroide Bennu resuelven un misterio que llevaba años desconcertando a los científicos
item.description: Cuando la sonda OSIRIS-REx, de la NASA, llegó a su destino en el asteroide Bennu en 2018, se encontró con algo inesperado. Según las mediciones tomadas por el telescopio Spitzer en 2007, este asteroide se calienta mucho cuando está expuesto a la radiación solar y se enfría igual de rápido por la noche. Esto es algo que en la Tierra ocurre en zonas que están cubiertas por roca fina, como la arena de playa. Por eso, pensaron que tocar la superficie y tomar muestras sería coser y cantar. En cambio, el lugar en el que trabajó la nave tenía una orografía complicada, con rocas de gran tamaño. Más… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: Single optical element combines soft X-ray imaging and spectroscopy
item.description: An international research team from Germany, Switzerland and Japan has demonstrated in a recent study that a single reflection zone plate (RZP) can perform both soft X-ray imaging and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) mapping. The approach could simplify future instruments that need to determine both where structures are located in a material and how their electronic properties vary. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Simulations reveal design rules for high-performance DNA particle motors
item.description: DNA-nano/microparticle motors are among the fastest artificial molecular motors reported to date, moving at approximately 30 nm per second. However, they are still slower than natural motor proteins (approximately 100–1,000 nm per second), and further improvements in design and performance are required. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Shared aquifers, border hotspots: Cooperation should follow where groundwater is pumped, scientists say
item.description: Groundwater depletion and groundwater-dependent irrigation tend to concentrate close to international borders within aquifers shared by two or more countries, where pumping on one side is more likely to affect users on the other, according to a publication by the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Keeping water molecules connected reduces carbon electrode corrosion
item.description: Carbon is inexpensive, conductive, and widely used in technologies such as fuel cells and water electrolyzers. But under strongly oxidizing conditions, carbon electrodes gradually corrode. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Using a range of advanced characterization techniques, researchers say they have developed a novel method with the potential to produce hydrogen from seawater using a process that requires less energy, resists corrosion and could support more economical hydrogen production. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research finds frequent disease outbreaks in B.C. salmon farms, endangering wild salmon
item.description: A new study with unprecedented access to Atlantic salmon farms in British Columbia raises urgent questions about the federal government's approach to regulating salmon farms and highlights disease risk to wild salmon populations. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Botanists comb Gabon's rich rainforests with nature on the line
item.description: Each year, Gabon's lush rainforests yield the discovery of previously unknown plant species to botanists like Archange Boupoya—who believes that this exceptional yet largely mysterious natural wealth needs to be cataloged to be saved. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What is 'human composting'—and how does it work?
item.description: What should happen to your body after you die? It's hardly a topic you'd bring up over dinner, but it's a decision that will eventually need to be made, either by you or by those you leave behind. Fuente: Phys.org.
